For example, one useful working distinction is along the lines of operational cadence, separating information into static, semi-static, and dynamic categories. All three categories are important to capture in information sharing frameworks. Government to government information sharing carries different risks and responsibilities from operator to operator information sharing. On space accessibility, Chile established the Scientific and Technical Commission on Satellite Matters, which will provide advice to the Ministry of Science with regard to projects which could be developed in the satellite infrastructure administered by the Chilean Air Force. With this, universities and research centres will be able to link their work with the national space system and the priorities of the national space policy. In terms of regional cooperation, Chile makes its National Space Center available as a platform for regional cooperation to develop technology, as well as to carry out the assembly, integration and testing of satellites, and also in order to monitor and track assets and to process information through advanced supercomputing capacity. In addition to other studies and forms of research which require controlled environments in a clean room, this infrastructure could support technical training, exchange of experience and cooperation with countries from Latin America and the Caribbean who are seeking to strengthen their own space programs and at the same time strengthen their knowledge and development of the region. For Chile, the Space 2030 agenda should contribute to more states participating in the peaceful use of space with their own capacity. Our country is making progress in this direction through a space policy which is being implemented, operative national infrastructure and a scientific and manufacturing ecosystem which is beginning to expand. Thank you very much, Madam.

Mr. Chair, following the mid-term review report submitted at the 68th session, my delegation wishes to share the Republic of Korea's follow-up activities centered on the four pillars of the Space 2030 agenda. To begin with, our commitment to fostering a robust space economy was demonstrated by the fourth flight of the Nuri launch vehicle in November 2025. This marked our first privately led launch, opening a new chapter in the commercialization of our space industry. Looking ahead, we are currently preparing for the fifth launch in the third quarter of this year, while further expanding our space transportation capabilities by developing a reusable launch vehicle. In our pursuits to enrich the space society, three scientific payloads aboard the next-generation MIST-I satellite 3 have been operating seamlessly since their launch in November 2025. These instruments are successfully gathering valuable data across diverse fields, including the space environment, space plasma, space medicine, and bio-3D printing. Furthermore, the next generation mid-size satellite two launched in May 2026 and Comsat seven launched in December 2025 have commenced nominal operations significantly enhancing our earth observation capacity. Concurrently, advancing space accessibility remains a core priority. The development of the Korean positioning system is in full swing towards the launch of its first satellite in 2029. And in October 2025, we successfully hosted the 19th meeting of the International Committee on Global Navigation Satellite Systems in Busan, demonstrating our active contribution to this platform under the auspices of the United Nations. In parallel, the Danuri lunar orbiter continues its mission successfully, contributing to international cooperation and data sharing efforts in lunar exploration. In the realm of space diplomacy, the Republic of Korea remains committed to promoting space education, engaging the next generation of space professionals, and advancing the meaningful participation of women in the space sector through the Space for Youth and Space for Women initiatives.
